content: The Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) guidelines focus on community-level interventions to address declines in intrinsic capacity, particularly mobility loss, among older adults. A scoping question was posed to determine whether physical exercise training, such as progressive resistance training or multimodal exercise, provides benefits or causes harm for older individuals with limitations in activities of daily living (ADLs). A recent meta-analysis of 54 studies revealed that 39% of individuals over 65 years of age experience limitations in ADLs, a prevalence three times higher than that observed in working-age groups. With advancing age, the ability to perform basic activities declines, but this decline is not uniform and is influenced by environmental factors. Population studies indicate that up to 20% of older adults can improve their functional capacity through exercise interventions, and many transition between high and low capacity within the same age group. This dynamic nature highlights the potential for restoring and maintaining optimal physical capacity, even in the oldest age groups. Evidence strongly associates reduced ability to perform basic activities with adverse outcomes, including premature mortality, institutionalization, increased risk of falls, depression, cognitive impairment, and decreased quality of life. Intervention trials involving multimodal physical exercise training targeting modifiable risk factors, such as strength and balance, have demonstrated significant benefits for older adults with reduced physical capacity, even among the very old and severely impaired. Simple physical activities, such as walking, have been shown to significantly reduce the need for assistance in daily activities. Additionally, earlier reviews provide empirical support for the positive effects of exercise on behavior, cognition, communication, and functioning in older adults with cognitive impairments. Understanding the impact of physical exercise on older adults with physical and cognitive limitations is crucial. To evaluate its benefits, evidence was reviewed on the effects of physical exercise on muscle strength, balance, gait speed, chair stand performance, timed up-and-go tests, ADLs, and physical functioning as measured by the Short Physical Performance Battery. While evidence from developed countries suggests the potential benefits of physical activity programs for older adults, it remains unclear whether these findings and recommendations are applicable to older individuals in low-resource healthcare settings, where the majority of the world's older population resides. The ICOPE guidelines utilized a systematic review process to assess the effects of various exercise interventions. Studies were identified through electronic databases such as Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. A recent search in October 2015 updated the literature sources. Systematic reviews included in the analysis focused on older adults with physical or cognitive limitations and evaluated outcomes such as muscle strength, balance, gait speed, chair stand performance, timed up-and-go tests, overall physical functioning, ADLs, and fall prevention. For example, Cadore et al. conducted a systematic review of the effects of different exercise interventions on fall risk, gait ability, and balance in physically frail older adults. Their review included 20 studies published between 1990 and 2012, with participants aged 72 to 83 years. The exercise duration ranged from 10 weeks to 1 year, and interventions included multimodal and progressive resistance exercises. Chou et al. performed a meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of exercise on physical function, ADLs, and quality of life in frail older adults. Their review included eight trials with 1,068 participants, with one trial specifically added to the ICOPE scope review. This trial involved a 48-week t’ai chi intervention for participants with a mean age of 81 years. Daniels et al. reviewed interventions to prevent disability in community-dwelling frail older adults. Their review included 10 studies, three of which were selected for the ICOPE scope review. These trials involved participants aged 77 to 81 years, with exercise durations ranging from 12 weeks to 10 months, and all utilized multimodal exercise. De Vries et al. conducted a meta-analysis on the effects of physical exercise therapy on mobility, physical functioning, physical activity, and quality of life in community-dwelling older adults with mobility limitations. Their review included 18 studies, four of which were added to the ICOPE scope review. These trials involved participants aged 75 to 78 years, with exercise durations ranging from 5 weeks to 1 year, and all employed multimodal exercise. Giné-Garriga et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis on physical exercise for improving performance-based measures of physical function in frail older adults living in the community. Their review included 19 trials, two of which were added to the ICOPE scope review. These trials involved participants aged 70 and 83 years, with exercise durations of 12 weeks to 1 year, and both used multimodal exercise. Howe et al. conducted a Cochrane systematic review of exercise interventions targeting balance in older adults. Their review included studies from various databases, such as MEDLINE and EMBASE, and focused on interventions to improve balance and reduce fall risk in older populations. Overall, the evidence supports the use of physical exercise interventions, particularly multimodal and progressive resistance exercises, to improve physical function, reduce fall risk, and enhance quality of life in older adults, including those with frailty or cognitive impairments. However, further research is needed to determine the applicability of these findings in low-resource settings.
